snapshot.title: SSC Polity: Important Articles & Amendments
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ SSC GK Hook: 368: Amend. 61st: Vote 18. 110: Money. 148: CAG. 280: FC. 352/356/360: Emergency. 73: Panchayat.

quick_notes.title: Emergency Provisions
quick_notes.detail: Art 352 (National), Art 356 (State/President's Rule), Art 360 (Financial - Never used in India).
quick_notes.explanation: Emergency Provisions are special powers that allow the central government to take control during a crisis. There are three types of emergency in India. Article 352, called National Emergency, lets the central government take over the entire country if there is a war, external attack, or armed rebellion. Article 356, known as President's Rule or State Emergency, allows the central government to take over a state government if the state cannot run according to the Constitution. Article 360, called Financial Emergency, gives the central government power to control the country's money and economy, but this has never been used in India. During any emergency, the central government becomes much stronger, and some of your Fundamental Rights (basic freedoms guaranteed to every citizen) can be suspended.

quick_notes.title: Constitutional Amendments (Art 368)
quick_notes.explanation: The Constitution of India can be changed through a process called an amendment, which is described in Article 368 (Article 368). An amendment is a formal change or addition made to the written rules of the Constitution. The First Amendment added a Ninth Schedule, which is a special list of laws that cannot be challenged in court. The Forty-Second Amendment is called the "Mini Constitution" because it made many big changes, including adding the words "Socialist" and "Secular" to the Preamble. The Forty-Fourth Amendment removed the Right to Property (Article 31) from the list of Fundamental Rights (FR), which are basic rights guaranteed to every citizen, and made it a simple legal right. The Fifty-Second Amendment added the Anti-Defection law, which stops elected members from changing their political party without losing their seat. The Sixty-First Amendment lowered the minimum voting age from 21 years to 18 years. The Seventy-Third and Seventy-Fourth Amendments created a formal system of local self-government called Panchayats (for villages) and Municipalities (for towns and cities). The One Hundred and First Amendment introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST), which is a single tax on the supply of goods and services across the whole country.

quick_notes.title: Top Articles to Memorize
quick_notes.detail: 108 (Joint Sitting), 110 (Money Bill), 112 (Budget), 148 (CAG), 280 (Finance Commission), 312 (All India Services), 324 (Election Commission).
quick_notes.explanation: Article 108 of the Constitution allows both houses of Parliament to meet together in a joint sitting to resolve a disagreement on a bill, but this does not apply to money bills or constitutional amendments. Article 110 defines a Money Bill as a bill that deals only with specific financial matters like taxes, government borrowing, or spending from the Consolidated Fund of India. Article 112 requires the government to present a statement of estimated receipts and expenditures for the coming year, which is called the annual financial statement or the Budget. Article 148 establishes the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, or CAG, who is the independent auditor of all government accounts. Article 280 sets up the Finance Commission every five years to recommend how tax money should be shared between the central government and the state governments. Article 312 allows Parliament to create All India Services, such as the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and Indian Police Service (IPS), which are common to both the centre and the states. Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the Election Commission of India, which is an independent body that conducts free and fair elections.

quick_notes.title: Official Languages (Art 343)
quick_notes.detail: Hindi in Devanagari script. 8th Schedule has 22 languages.
quick_notes.explanation: Official Languages (Article 343 of the Indian Constitution) Article 343 of the Indian Constitution declares that the official language of the Union government of India is Hindi, written in the Devanagari script. This means all central government communications, laws, and official documents are primarily in this language. However, the Constitution also protects other languages by listing them in the Eighth Schedule, which currently contains 22 languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Tamil, Urdu, and others. These scheduled languages are recognized for official purposes at the state level and for cultural preservation, but Hindi remains the sole official language for the central government. The use of English for official purposes was allowed to continue for 15 years after the Constitution came into effect in 1950, and it is still used alongside Hindi in many government functions today.

quick_notes.title: Panchayati Raj (73rd Amend)
quick_notes.detail: Art 243. 3-tier system: Gram, Block, District. Added 11th Schedule. Nagarpalika (74th) added 12th Schedule.
quick_notes.explanation: Panchayati Raj is a system of local self-government for villages and rural areas in India, established by the 73rd Amendment to the Constitution in 1992. This amendment added Part IX to the Constitution, which contains Article 243, and it creates a three-tier structure of councils: the Gram Panchayat at the village level, the Panchayat Samiti or Block Panchayat at the intermediate level, and the Zila Parishad or District Panchayat at the district level. The amendment also added the Eleventh Schedule, which is a list of 29 subjects that these village councils can manage, such as agriculture, education, and drinking water. Separately, the 74th Amendment, also passed in 1992, deals with Nagarpalikas, which are local governments for towns and cities, and it added the Twelfth Schedule, a list of 18 subjects for these urban councils, like urban planning and fire services.
